abstract: Biological aging progresses at different rates across individuals, yet identifying the molecular determinants underlying this variation remains a central challenge. Using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing and transcriptomic profiling of hepatic tissue from the model fish species, Japanese medaka (Oryzias latipes), we develop and compare epigenetic and transcriptomic aging clocks to assess how distinct molecular modalities capture aging signals across the lifespan. Both clocks accurately predict chronological age, although CpG methylation-based models outperform those derived from gene expression. Critically, the relative age acceleration metrics from these two clocks are largely uncorrelated, indicating that they capture distinct facets of biological aging. Despite this lack of correlated aging signal, age-associated changes in DNA methylation and gene expressions display patterns of spatial overlap, suggesting localized regulatory interactions. Genetic association scans of sequenced exomes identify variants associated with age acceleration metrics. In particular, variants within a region containing nfixb and rad23a exert strong effects on epigenetic age estimates, a finding which is validated in an independent cohort. Age-associated methylation at nfixb transcription start sites, together with genotype-specific effects on methylation and exon usage, implicate nfixb as a modifier of epigenetic aging. Comparative methylome analyses reveal conserved age-related methylation at nfixb/Nfix in medaka and mice, and is consistent with recent findings implicating a role for NF1 transcription factors in human epigenetic aging. Collectively, these findings show epigenetic and transcriptomic clocks capture distinct aging dimensions shaped by genetic and stochastic factors. They highlight the modular architecture of aging and position medaka as a powerful model for dissecting conserved mechanisms of vertebrate aging.
